newsitem.title: USA: U.S. delays ruling in tomato dispute with Mexico.
newsitem.headline: U.S. delays ruling in tomato dispute with Mexico.

text.p: The Commerce Department Tuesday postponed a key ruling in a controversial anti-dumping case brought by Florida tomato growers against Mexico until Oct. 28.

In a notice to be published in the Federal Register Wednesday, the International Trade Administration, a branch of the Commerce Department, said the extra time was "necessary to consider certain novel issues raised by the parties."
The Commerce Department was expected to release its preliminary ruling Tuesday on whether Mexico was selling tomatoes in the United States at below-market prices.

The ruling will be important to Florida tomato growers, who brought the controversial trade complaint against Mexico earlier this year to protect their share of the domestic winter vegetable market. Florida poducers have charged they have lost more than $400 million in business because of Mexico's selling practices.
Officials representing the Florida tomato growers said they were disappointed with the delay, but supported it if the agency needed more time to thoroughly study the issue.

We're suppportive and we're disappointed," said Ray Gilmer of the Florida Fruit & Vegetable Association. "But if it's in the interests of making the right decision, we're willing to wait another 20 days."
Officials close to the issue were careful not to interpret the agency's action as negative or positive for either side.
"Extensions in dumping cases are quite common," said Terry Stewart, the lead attorney representing the U.S. industry.

The issue has been a political football in this election year. Critics of the U.S. complaint have said that Florida's 25 electoral votes have caused the administration to look more sympathetically at the U.S. grower's position.

The dispute has also divided the normally cohesive U.S. agricultural community. Groups representing such commodities as corn and livestock have strongly opposed the complaint due to fears that the dispute will hurt trade with Mexico.

Mexico is a major market for U.S. farmers and is projected to buy more than $60 billion worth of American farm goods this year, up more than 30 percent from a few years ago when the North American Free Trade Agreement was implemented.
If the International Trade Administration rules in favor of the U.S. industry, sanctions -- which could include tariffs or quotas -- could eventually be imposed on imports of Mexican tomatoes.
Mexico has threatened to retaliate against other U.S. agricultural products if action is taken against its growers.

Consumer groups have also objected to the complaint, claiming that import tariffs on Mexican produce, or a drop in available tomatoes because of the tariffs, could hike tomato prices for U.S. consumers.
